title: The 2026 admin skills reset: what assistants need beyond Microsoft Office
dek: Office software remains useful, but the stronger career signal is now the ability to use AI safely, check its work and know when human judgement must take over.
body_html:
An administrator can now turn a transcript into meeting notes in seconds. The valuable part starts after generation: are the names, dates and decisions correct? Has confidential information been handled properly? Is the tone suitable for the people receiving it? Does the summary omit a disagreement that matters?

As generative tools spread through office work, producing a polished first draft is becoming less distinctive. Reliability is not. The emerging skills reset for administrators is therefore less about becoming an AI specialist and more about becoming a capable supervisor of AI-assisted work.

The shift is already visible. In late September 2025, 23% of UK businesses told the Office for National Statistics that they were using some form of AI. Among businesses planning to adopt AI within three months, or unsure whether they would, 27% expected administrative or clerical roles to be the most affected. However, 36% expected to train or retrain existing staff, compared with 12% expecting to automate or replace roles and 8% expecting to recruit new staff with AI skills. These figures do not predict what will happen to any individual job, but they do suggest that many existing administrators will be asked to absorb new workflows. The ONS data provides the full context.

What AI literacy means in an admin job

Skills England’s July 2026 annual report describes practical AI literacy as the ability to use, verify and safely integrate AI tools. It also reports employer demand for judgement, problem-solving, collaboration, digital fluency and responsible AI use. The report is careful to acknowledge that adoption remains uneven and its effects uncertain.

The practical conclusion is not that Word, Excel, Outlook or Teams no longer matter. Administrators still need to operate the systems their organisations use. The change is that software proficiency alone does not show whether someone can manage an AI-assisted process safely and accurately.

For an administrator, useful AI literacy can be divided into six capabilities.

  1. Giving clear instructions. A useful prompt states the task, relevant context, permitted source material, constraints, required format and checks. For example: summarise the attached approved notes into an action list, preserve exact dates and names, identify any unclear ownership, and do not add information that is not in the notes.
  2. Checking the output. Verification means comparing names, numbers, dates, quotations, actions and conclusions with the original source. It also means noticing what is missing. A fluent answer is not evidence that the answer is correct.
  3. Handling information safely. An administrator should know which tools are approved, what information may be entered, which privacy settings apply and when permission is needed. Sensitive material should not be placed into an unapproved service simply because it makes the task faster.
  4. Choosing suitable tasks. Drafting an agenda from approved notes is different from deciding how to respond to a grievance, complaint or personnel issue. Good judgement includes recognising when a task is too sensitive, ambiguous or consequential for unsupervised automation.
  5. Turning data into a useful message. Producing a chart is not the same as explaining what it means. Administrators increasingly need to identify a pattern, check the underlying figures and present the implication clearly to a manager or team.
  6. Coordinating people. AI cannot remove the need to clarify ownership, negotiate diary conflicts, follow up tactfully or understand why a stakeholder has not replied. Collaboration and relationship management remain central to effective administration.

These capabilities closely reflect the Skills England AI foundation skills benchmark. Its six foundation skills include writing clear instructions, supporting routine processes, using simple automation, adjusting tool settings, understanding risks and analysing information by checking outputs for accuracy and errors.

They also fit the broader hiring signals. LinkedIn’s 2026 UK Skills on the Rise analysis placed prompt engineering and data storytelling alongside cross-functional collaboration and relationship management. That combination matters. It suggests that technical confidence and human coordination should be developed together, rather than treated as competing skill sets. LinkedIn explains how it identified the emerging skills.

Do admin jobs now require Microsoft Copilot?

Some do, but it is not a universal requirement. PwC’s June 2026 UK AI Jobs Barometer counted specialist AI skills in 2.2% of UK job postings during 2025. It also found that occupations with the greatest AI exposure were experiencing roughly twice the skills transformation of the least-exposed occupations. This is evidence of rapid change, not evidence that every administrator needs the same product certification. PwC sets out the findings and methodology.

If the vacancies you want explicitly mention Microsoft 365 Copilot, learn how it works across Word, Outlook, Excel and Teams. The official Microsoft Learn introductory pathway is a sensible starting point.

Do not stop at the product name. The more transferable claim is that you can use an approved AI tool to complete a defined task, provide good context, verify the result and escalate uncertainty. That evidence remains useful when an employer changes software.

How to add AI skills to an admin CV

Avoid adding “AI” as an unsupported keyword next to Microsoft Office. Show the workflow, the checks and the outcome. Only use statements that are true, and only include time or cost savings that you can substantiate.

  • Meeting support: Used an approved AI tool to prepare first-pass meeting summaries, then checked actions, owners and deadlines against the source notes before circulation.
  • Prompting: Created reusable prompt templates for agendas, internal updates and document summaries, with defined formats and verification steps.
  • Process improvement: Identified repetitive reminder and information-sorting tasks suitable for automation while retaining human approval for external communication.
  • Data communication: Combined spreadsheet analysis with AI-assisted drafting to turn operational data into concise, source-checked management updates.
  • Responsible use: Followed organisational rules on approved tools, confidential information and human review when using AI-supported workflows.

In an interview, be ready to explain one example from beginning to end: the problem, the information used, the prompt or automation, what you checked, what went wrong and where you retained human control. A small, credible example is stronger than a broad claim to be an AI expert.

How to choose AI training for administration

The best course is not necessarily the one with the longest syllabus or the most impressive badge. Look for training that covers a real administrative workflow and includes verification, privacy, risk and judgement.

Skills England’s June 2026 employer guide emphasises practical, contextualised and accessible learning. It recommends covering technical skills, non-technical application and responsible or ethical use together. The guidance is based on workshops, case studies and a UK-wide employer survey.

A useful training sequence is:

  1. Learn the foundation. Use the government benchmark to identify gaps. The AI Skills Boost programme offers free courses designed for different roles and levels of technical experience.
  2. Practise one low-risk workflow. Choose meeting preparation, information organisation, an internal email draft or a routine spreadsheet summary.
  3. Build a verification checklist. Record what must be checked, which source is authoritative and who approves the final output.
  4. Add product training when relevant. Learn Copilot or another named tool if it appears repeatedly in your target vacancies or is used by your employer.
  5. Keep evidence. Create a sanitised portfolio showing the task, prompt structure, review process and lesson learned. Do not include employer-confidential material.

The next move

Choose one routine task you already understand well. Write down how it is completed now, where mistakes would matter and which parts could be assisted safely. Then test an approved tool and document your checks.

That exercise develops the skill employers are likely to value most: not simply using AI, but applying it with enough judgement that other people can trust the work.
